claims.text: Moderate sliding wear in a neutral chloride electrolyte selectively enriches Al and other passivating elements at the worn surface.
Selective enrichment of passivating elements during sliding produces a stable, self-adaptive tribofilm.
Formation of the stable tribofilm lowers overall degradation relative to conditions in which the film is absent or destroyed.
An Al-alloyed AlxCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy can be optimized for passive-film formation.
Adjusting sliding speed and load can establish moderate wear conditions that favor tribofilm formation.
The in-situ tribofilm consists of wear debris selectively enriched in Al and other passivating elements.
Mechanical wear generates a debris layer that becomes enriched in passivating elements.
The enriched debris layer protects the underlying surface from aggressive corrosion.
The tribofilm can accommodate continued mechanical removal.
The balance between tribofilm formation and removal governs overall tribo-corrosion degradation.
Minimal wear limits tribofilm formation and consequently gives higher overall degradation than successful moderate-wear film formation.
Excessive wear destroys the tribofilm and consequently gives higher overall degradation than successful moderate-wear film formation.
Very high sliding speeds or loads inhibit tribofilm formation and increase the degradation rate.
The proposed mechanism requires an alloy composition capable of selective passivation and wear conditions that permit controlled tribofilm formation.
Overly aggressive wear or insufficient enrichment in passivating elements can prevent the proposed protective mechanism.
